doc.title: Evan Christopher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 1, 2009

chapter: Coming to New Orleans and the clarinet tradition
title: Arriving in New Orleans in July 1994: work, peers and acceptance
summary: He arrived with no expectations and was surprised by how quickly he found work and a community of young peers. After a year and a half he felt limits on the music and grew defensive about style elements.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Did you have preconceptions about what New Orleans was going to be like, and how were they met when you got there?

No. I didn’t have any preconceptions about it. It was like when I woke up there, in the context of this tour that I was on, I think we drove all night from Chicago as a matter of fact. We’d had a job in Chicago and I think we drove the whole night to wake up in the morning. This was in July of 1994. And it really was like nowhere else I’d ever been. It was — the air was in a way like nothing I’d ever felt. I mean I knew what humidity was, I’d been to Washington, D.C. once in the summertime and I’d been places, but this was different. Different smells, different — so much of it was different. I didn’t have expectations. I was surprised how quickly I had work, almost as much work as I wanted.

I was surprised at how quickly I found a community of peers, young guys, some definitely were younger than me, some guys a few years older than me, that could sit around a restaurant at breakfast and talk about CDs we just bought and stuff like that, and, “Oh you got the new Louis Armstrong box set?” So I think that there’s a level of community that surprised me, there was a level of acceptance that was a little disarming and I still don’t know what to do with that aspect of it.
Were those people that were so accepting of you all natives?

And at the time I don’t think I made as much of a distinction. But that was disarming. So no, I didn’t have any expectations. There was a point, pretty soon though, within only a year and a half or so, where I was already — definitely not bored — but I definitely felt like okay, well all right, there didn’t seem to be this infinite ceiling or it didn’t seem like there were infinite possibilities for the music, at least not in the context that I was in. I didn’t see that yet. I wasn’t really acutely aware of what was happening creatively. I spent a year and a half just seeing what I could do with New Orleans music and how quickly I could kind of find a way to apply or feel like I was anchored in what to me represented a very specific tradition with very style-specific elements to it, to the point where I got very defensive when those elements weren’t there.
